passages.title: The night vigil and the weighty revelation
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are Allah calling His Messenger ﷺ out from under his blanket in the earliest days of prophethood — up, into the night, into the Qur'an. They hold together as one instruction with a reason attached: ayat 1–4 give the command (rise, stand through the night — half of it, or a little less, or a little more — and recite with *tartīl*), and ayah 5 gives the why — **a weighty word is coming to you**. The vigil is the training; the revelation is what it trains him to carry.

## The man in the blanket

*Muzzammil* means, literally, "one wrapped up in clothes"; its near-synonym *muddaththir* opens the next sūrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the Prophet ﷺ is addressed here with reference to a particular way he had wrapped himself.

The first such moment came at the cave of Ḥirāʼ. The first revelation was, in Maʿārif's words, a hard experience: he was seized with a shivering cold, and when he reached home he asked Khadījah (may Allah be pleased with her) to wrap him in a blanket, and she did — Maʿārif notes that Bukhari reports this event in detail in the very first chapter of his book. Some narrations mention another occasion: when the pagans of Makkah accused him of being a magician who separated friends from one another, he felt aggrieved and wrapped himself in his clothes out of grief.

Related to this is the break in revelation (*fatrat al-waḥy*, the period in which revelation paused). Maʿārif cites the narration of Jābir (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: while walking, he heard a voice from heaven, looked up, and saw the angel who had appeared to him at Ḥirāʼ sitting on a chair between heaven and earth; he was struck with awe, returned home and said, *"Wrap me up, wrap me up" (zammilūnī, zammilūnī)* — and Allah revealed the first five verses of Sūrah al-Muddaththir. [Bukhari and Muslim]

So both titles — the wrapped one and the enveloped one — belong to a real posture of a real man on a real night. Maʿārif (quoting Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī) says both forms of address are used affectionately and endearingly to console him; Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani calls it "a loving style adopted by Allah Taʿālā to console him." Feel the tenderness of it: not "O Prophet," not "O Messenger," but the ordinary human posture of that moment, named gently — and then the command.

Ibn Kathir records how the early authorities read the address. Ibn ʿAbbās, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and as-Suddī all said it means "O you who are asleep"; Qatādah said it means "the one who is wrapped up in his garments." Ibn Kathir's own summary: Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to cease being wrapped up — to stop being covered during the night — and to get up and stand in prayer to his Lord. He connects it to the description of the believers elsewhere: *"Their sides forsake their beds, to invoke their Lord in fear and hope"* (32:16).

## When standing at night was an obligation

To feel the weight of ayah 2 you have to know where in the Prophet's ﷺ life it lands. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a consensus of scholarly opinion — read partly from the very titles *muzzammil* and *muddaththir* — that this sūrah belongs to the earliest period, before the five daily prayers had been made obligatory; those were prescribed on the night of the Ascent (*miʿrāj*, the Prophet's ﷺ ascent to the heavens).

Here the commentators differ, and it is worth naming the difference rather than smoothing it. Ibn Kathir holds that this night standing "was obligatory upon him alone," citing *"And in some parts of the night offer the Ṣalāh with it, as an additional prayer for you"* (17:79). Maʿārif, on the authority of Imam Baghawī and on the basis of aḥādīth reported by ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) and others, holds that the night prayer was compulsory for the Prophet ﷺ **and** the whole Muslim community until the five prayers were prescribed.

The central narration behind all of this is ʿĀ'ishah's answer to Saʿīd bin Hishām, recorded by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad, with Muslim recording similarly in his Ṣaḥīḥ. He asked her about the Prophet's ﷺ character and she replied, *"Have you not read the Qur'an? … Verily, the character of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the Qur'an."* Then he asked about his night prayer, and she said: *"Have you not read the Sūrah, 'Yā ayyuhal-Muzzammil'? Verily, Allah made standing at night obligatory at the beginning of this Sūrah. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions stood for an entire year during the night until their feet swelled. Allah held back the revelation of the end of this Sūrah for twelve months. Then Allah revealed the lightening of this burden at the end of this Sūrah. Then the standing for night prayer became voluntary after it used to be obligatory."*

Ibn Jarir records the same from Abu ʿAbdur-Raḥmān — that when ayah 1 was revealed the people stood in night prayer for a year "until their feet and shins swelled," until *"So recite of it what is easy"* (73:20) came down, "then the people relaxed"; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and as-Suddī said the same. And Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah, said of ayat 2–3: *"This became difficult on the believers. Then Allah lightened the matter for them and had mercy on them"* — and after quoting the concession at the end of the sūrah he added, *"So Allah made the matter easy — and unto Him is due all praise — and He did not make matters difficult."*

Maʿārif adds that this repeal is transmitted by Abu Dawud and Nasa'i on the authority of ʿĀ'ishah, and reports from Ibn ʿAbbās (via Mazhari) that when the five prayers became obligatory on the night of the *miʿrāj*, the obligatory character of *tahajjud* — the night vigil prayer, *ṣalāt at-tahajjud* — was abrogated, but retained as *sunnah*, because the Prophet ﷺ performed it most regularly, as did most of the Companions.

So read ayat 2–4 knowing both halves of the story: a year of swollen feet, and then mercy.

## How much of the night? (ayat 2–4)

Maʿārif walks through the arithmetic carefully. In ayah 2, *al-layl* carries the definite article, so it means **the entire night**: stand the whole night except a little of it. But "a little" is left indefinite — so ayah 3 and the opening of ayah 4 clarify it: *half of it, or make it a little less, or make it a little more.*

Ibn Kathir reads "half of it" as "instead of the whole night," and paraphrases: *We have commanded you to stand in prayer for half of the night, either a little more than it or a little less. There is no hardship on you concerning that* slight increase or decrease.

Maʿārif raises the obvious objection: how can "a little" be *half*? Its answer is that the early part of the night is already spent in the Maghrib and ʿIshāʼ prayers; "half" therefore means half of what remains of the night, and that, measured against the whole night, does amount to "a little." Working the sums, Maʿārif concludes that what was compulsory was standing for at least a little over one quarter of a night.

Notice what the wording does emotionally: Allah gives him a band, not a stopwatch. Half, or somewhat under, or somewhat over — the exactness of the hour was never the point.

## "And recite the Qur'an with tartīl" (ayah 4)

This is where the passage's language repays close attention. Maʿārif cites Imam Rāghib in *al-Mufradāt*: *tartīl* originally means "to put together and arrange well the component parts of a word and speech and make it distinct." The purport, Maʿārif says, is that the Qur'an must not be recited in haste but in a leisurely manner — distinctly, deliberately, in a well-measured tone — and at the same time one must reflect on its meaning and message (Mazhari).

There is a grammatical point too. *Wa rattil* is conjoined to *qumi-l-layl*, so it describes what is to be done **in** the night prayer. And although that prayer contains *tasbīḥ*, bowing and prostration, the ayah indicates that its basic component is the recitation of the Qur'an — which is why, as Maʿārif notes, the authentic reports show the Prophet's ﷺ *tahajjud* being very greatly prolonged, a pattern the Companions and their students followed.

Ibn Kathir's gloss is simply: recite it slowly, "for that will help in understanding the Qur'an and contemplating it." He then shows what that sounded like:

- ʿĀ'ishah said, *"He used to recite the chapter slowly, so much so that it would be longer than chapters that were actually longer than it."*
- In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhari, Anas was asked about the Messenger's ﷺ recitation and replied, *"He used to elongate the letters"* — then recited *Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm*, stretching each of the three phrases.
- Umm Salamah, asked the same, said, *"He used to pause in his recitation, verse by verse,"* and demonstrated with the opening ayat of al-Fātiḥah. Ibn Kathir says this was recorded by Ahmad, Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi. Maʿārif reports the same incident with the detail that in her rendering "every single letter was clear and distinct" [Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud, Nasa'i — as quoted by Mazhari].

**Beauty of voice belongs to tartīl.** Ibn Kathir cites, without naming a collection in this passage, the Prophet's ﷺ words to beautify the Qur'an with one's voice, that whoever does not chant nicely with the Qur'an is not of us, and his remark about Abu Mūsā having been given "a windpipe from the windpipes of the family of Dāwūd" — to which Abu Mūsā replied, *"If I knew that you had been listening to my recitation, I would have truly beautified it for you."* Maʿārif adds a narration of Abu Hurayrah that Allah does not listen to any recitation as much as He listens to the recitation of a Prophet who recites with a beautiful voice (cited from Mazhari).

**And haste is its opposite.** Ibn Masʿūd said: *"Do not scatter the Qur'an out like the scattering of sand, and do not rush through it like the hasty recitation of poetry. Stop at its amazing parts and make your heart move with it. None of you should let his concern be to reach the end of the chapter."* (recorded by al-Baghawī). Al-Bukhari records from Abī Wā'il that a man told Ibn Masʿūd he had recited the whole of the Mufaṣṣal — Qāf to an-Nās — in a single rakʿah, and Ibn Masʿūd answered, *"This is rushing like the haste of reciting poetry,"* then named twenty chapters of the Mufaṣṣal that the Prophet ﷺ used to pair, two to a rakʿah.

What is *tartīl* finally aiming at? Maʿārif answers with two reports from Qurtubi. ʿAlqamah saw a man reciting with a beautiful voice and exclaimed, *"He has recited the Qur'an with tartīl: may my parents be sacrificed to him!"* And al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed a man who was reciting an ayah of the Qur'an and weeping, and said to the people: have you heard Allah's command *"and recite the Qur'an with tartīl"*? — *"This is tartīl, which this person is doing."* Slowness of tongue is the method; a moved heart is the goal.

## "We will soon send upon you a weighty word" (ayah 5)

*Qawlan thaqīlan* — a heavy word. Ibn Kathir preserves more than one way of taking that heaviness, and they are not rivals so much as layers.

**Heavy in what it asks.** Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said it means "the actions with it." Maʿārif develops the same reading: the "weighty discourse" is the Qur'an, because its teachings of lawful and unlawful are permanently binding, and carrying them out is the weightiest task for human nature — "except those for whom Allah makes it easier."

**Heavy in the moment of its descent, because of its magnificence.** Zayd bin Thābit said, *"The Messenger of Allah ﷺ received some revelation while his thigh was on top of my thigh, and my thigh was almost crushed due to it."* Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr that he asked the Prophet ﷺ whether he felt anything when revelation came, and he replied, *"I hear a ringing and then I remain quiet when that occurs. There has not been a single time that revelation has come to me except that I thought that my soul was about to be taken."* — Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad was alone in narrating this. And at the beginning of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhari it is recorded from ʿĀ'ishah that al-Ḥārith bin Hishām asked how the revelation came, and the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and it is most severe upon me. Then this state passes away from me after I have grasped what is inspired. Sometimes the angel comes to me in the form of a man and talks to me and I grasp whatever he says."* ʿĀ'ishah added that she saw him receiving revelation and noticed the sweat dropping from his forehead on a very cold day. In another narration of hers recorded by Ahmad, if revelation came while he was on his riding animal, the animal's *jirān* — the bottom of its neck — would begin moving intensely.

**Both at once, and heavier still later.** Ibn Jarir chose the view that the revelation is heavy in both ways simultaneously. And ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam added a third horizon: *"Just as it is heavy in this world, it will also be heavy on the Day of Judgement in the Scales."*

Note also the tense. The wording is future — *We will soon send*. The vigil is being commanded before the weight arrives, not after.

## Why the night comes first

This is the thread that ties the five ayat into one, and Maʿārif states it plainly right here on ayah 5: the night prayer is prescribed so that a person becomes accustomed to the difficulty of waking at night — a struggle against excess sleep and the comfort of the lower self — and this exercise makes it easier to abide by the injunctions contained in the "weighty discourse," that is, the Qur'an.

Maʿārif says the same thing about the opening address itself: having been called by that affectionate title, the Prophet ﷺ is told that praying to Allah in the stillness of the night will prepare him for the heavy task entrusted to him. Command first, reason after — and the reason is that the night is where the weight becomes carryable.

## Living it

- **Depth over distance.** Everything in ayah 4 pushes against the instinct to measure recitation in pages. ʿĀ'ishah, in the same narration, said she did not know of the Prophet ﷺ ever reciting the entire Qur'an in one night before morning. A short sūrah recited slowly, understood, and felt is what the ayah asks for.
- **Consistency over intensity.** She also described the shape of his nights: his tooth-stick and water for ablution made ready, "and Allah would awaken him whenever He wished to awaken him during the night." She said that whenever he prayed a particular prayer he liked to remain consistent in its performance — and that if oversleeping, pain or illness kept him from the night prayer, he would pray twelve units during the day instead. Missing a night was met with making up, not giving up.
- **Take the concession Allah offered.** The obligation of the long vigil was lifted by Allah's own mercy at the end of this same sūrah: *"So recite of it what is easy."* Ibn ʿAbbās's comment is the right posture — Allah made the matter easy and did not make matters difficult. A small, steady portion of the night, held to over years, is exactly what the sūrah ends up asking of us.
- **This is training, not withdrawal from the world.** Maʿārif's reading keeps the two halves of the passage joined: the vigil is prescribed so that the injunctions of the weighty discourse become easier to carry — which means it is preparation for a life lived among people, not an escape from it. In the very narration that carries ʿĀ'ishah's account, men who had resolved to leave their wives for worship and fighting were told by the Prophet ﷺ, *"Is there not for you all an excellent example in me?"* — and he made them take their wives back.

passages.title: The night's deeper mark and undivided devotion
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is doing.** Ayat 1–5 gave the command — rise at night, recite the Qur'an slowly. Ayat 6 and 7 give the *wisdom* behind that command, and ayat 8–10 open it outwards into a whole way of living: unbroken remembrance and undivided devotion (8), the One who owns east and west (9), and patience under what those who reject him say (10).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, at ayah 9, quotes Imam Yaʿqūb Karkhī: from the beginning of the surah up to that verse there is reference to the *maqāmāt as-sulūk* — the stations of the spiritual path. He lists five: [1] solitude at night to worship Allah; [2] preoccupation with the Qur'an; [3] constant remembrance of Allah; [4] severance of relationship with everything-other-than-Allah; [5] total trust in Allah. Ayah 9 is, in Maʿārif's counting, the fifth injunction given to the Prophet ﷺ in this surah.

## The year these ayat were lived

Ibn Kathir records — from Imam Ahmad's *Musnad*, noting that Muslim recorded similarly in his *Sahih* — the account of Saʿīd ibn Hishām, who asked ʿĀ'ishah about the Prophet's ﷺ night prayer. She answered: "Have you not read the Surah *Yā ayyuhā'l-muzzammil*?" Allah made standing at night obligatory at the beginning of this surah, she said, "so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions stood for an entire year during the night until their feet swelled. Allah held back the revelation of the end of this Surah for twelve months. Then, Allah revealed the lightening of this burden at the end of this Surah. Then, the standing for night prayer became voluntary after it used to be obligatory."

Ibn Jarīr records the same from Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān — the people prayed a whole year until their feet and shins swelled, until Allah revealed *"So recite of it what is easy"* (73:20), "then the people relaxed." Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and as-Suddī said the same, and Ibn ʿAbbās (through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa) said it had become hard on the believers, "then Allah lightened the matter for them and had mercy on them."

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam places ayah 7 squarely inside that year: Allah said this, he explains, "when the (voluntary) night prayer was obligatory. Then, Allah blessed His servants, lightened the matter and removed its obligation."

## Ayah 6: what *nāshi'ah* actually means

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *nāshi'ah*, built on the pattern of *ʿāfiyah*, is a verbal noun meaning "to rise by night for prayer." The classical authorities read its scope differently:

- **ʿĀ'ishah**: to rise at night *after having slept* — that is, tahajjud.
- **Ibn Kaysān**: prayer in the later part of the night. **Ibn Zayd**: prayer in any part of the night. **Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī**: any prayer offered after ʿIshā'.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn az-Zubayr**, asked by Ibn Abī Mulaykah, answered simply: "The entire night is *nāshi'ah*." (Maʿārif reports this from Mazharī.)

Ibn Kathir reports the same spread — ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn az-Zubayr and Mujāhid said "the entire night is *nāshi'ah*"; in one narration Mujāhid said "after ʿIshā'," as did Abū Mijlaz, Qatādah, Sālim, Abū Ḥāzim and Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir. Ibn Kathir resolves it: *nāshi'ah* of the night refers to its **hours and its times** — every hour of it is called *nāshi'ah*.

Maʿārif agrees there is no conflict here. First, **performing any voluntary (nafl) prayer after ʿIshā' fulfils the sunnah requirement of *nāshi'ah* of the night and *qiyām* of the night**. Second, the constant practice of the Prophet ﷺ, of the overwhelming majority of his Companions and of the righteous predecessors of the ummah was to perform this prayer *in the later part of the night, after waking from sleep* — and therefore that time "is more virtuous, more meritorious and attracts more blessings."

## Why the night: *ashaddu waṭ'an wa aqwamu qīlā*

**أَشَدُّ وَطْئًا — *ashaddu waṭ'an*.** Read with *fatḥa* on the *wāw* (*waṭ'an*), Maʿārif explains, the word is an infinitive meaning "to subdue" or "to suppress": this time of night helps a person suppress his evil desires. This is the meaning adopted by Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī, and Maʿārif's translation is based on it.

In another *qirā'ah* the word is pronounced *wiṭā'an*, an infinitive meaning **"to conform."** The same root appears in *"so that they may conform (only) to the number of what Allah has sanctified"* (9:37). Ibn Zayd and Ibn ʿAbbās, Maʿārif notes, interpreted the word in that second sense here. **Ibn Zayd**: getting up in the night for prayer is the most effective means of making the heart, eye, ear and tongue mutually correspond and conform. **Ibn ʿAbbās**: at that hour there is the closest degree of conformity between the ear and the heart — because there is no noise when most people are asleep.

Ibn Kathir makes the same point: standing at night is "better for training the heart and the tongue… better for understanding it than in the recitation of the day."

**وَأَقْوَمُ قِيلًا — *aqwamu qīlā*.** *Aqwam* means "more upright." The recitation of the Qur'an, says Maʿārif, is more upright and concentrated at night, because there are no noises to distract the heart or the mind.

Ibn Kathir records: Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Yaʿlā al-Mawṣilī said: Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿīd al-Jawharī told us, that Abū Usāmah told us, that al-Aʿmash informed us — that Anas ibn Mālik recited this ayah as *"inna nāshi'ata'l-layli hiya ashaddu wa aṣwabu qīlā."* A man said to him, "We recite it *wa aqwamu qīlā*." Anas answered him: "Most correct (*aṣwab*), most suitable (*aqwam*), the best for preparation (*ahyā'*) and similar words are all the same" in meaning.

Maʿārif sums up: ayah 5 put forward the wisdom of night prayer **for the Prophet ﷺ specifically**. Ayah 6 puts forward its wisdom **for common people**, and Night-Prayer has for them two characteristics: [1] harmony between the heart and the tongue, and [2] peace of mind, which makes it easier to recite the Qur'an.

## Ayah 7: the long swim of the day

*Inna laka fi'n-nahāri sabḥan ṭawīlā.* The word *sabḥ*, Maʿārif explains, literally means "to flow, walk or move about," and from it we also get the sense of **swimming in water**. Here it signifies a long chain of engagements in the day: duties such as educating people, preaching to them, reforming humanity, performing domestic chores and discharging social responsibilities.

Maʿārif calls this the **third point of wisdom** as to why night prayer was enjoined, and says it relates both to the Prophet ﷺ and to the general body of the Muslim community: during the day it is difficult to concentrate on worship, so the night should be reserved for that purpose.

The early authorities gloss the word compatibly. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah and ʿAṭā' ibn Abī Muslim: "leisure time and sleep." Abu'l-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, Abū Mālik, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Sufyān ath-Thawrī: "a long amount of leisure time." Qatādah also said: "leisure, aspirations and activities." ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam puts it most directly: *"This means for your needs. Therefore, leave the night open for your religious devotion."*

Maʿārif adds the moderate note: **a person should sleep according to his need, and perform his night-prayer as well.**

## From the Sunnah: how he ﷺ actually did it

In the same narration from ʿĀ'ishah (Imam Ahmad's *Musnad*; Muslim recorded similarly in his *Sahih*), she described his night: "We used to prepare his *Siwāk* for him and his ablution water, and Allah would awaken him whenever He wished to awaken him during the night." He would clean his teeth and perform ablution, then pray eight rakʿahs, sitting during them only at the end of the eighth — and there he would sit and remember his Lord the Most High and supplicate to Him. Then he would stand without saying the *taslīm*, pray a ninth, sit and remember Allah and supplicate again, then say the greeting of peace audibly, then pray two more units while sitting: eleven in all. When he became older and heavier, he made it seven plus two — nine in all.

Three details carry as much weight as the numbers:

- **Consistency**: "Whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray a particular prayer, he liked to remain consistent in its performance."
- **Provision for failure**: if he were ever kept from the night prayer by oversleeping, pain or illness, "he would pray twelve units of supererogatory prayer during the day."
- **Restraint**: "I do not know of Allah's Prophet ﷺ ever reciting the entire Qur'an in one night before morning nor did he fast an entire month other than the month of Ramadan."

## Ayah 8: remembrance, and devotion that cuts loose

*Wadhkuri'sma rabbika wa tabattal ilayhi tabtīlā.* Maʿārif notes the grammar: "And remember the name of your Lord" is grammatically conjoined to *"Stand at night [for prayer]"* in ayah 2. But ayah 8 enjoins a devotional activity that **can be performed at any time of day or night**. Since it is inconceivable that the Prophet ﷺ would ever fail to remember Allah, the purport of the command (per Mazharī) is to emphasise **keeping to it consistently**.

This is possible, Maʿārif adds, only if "remembering Allah" is taken in its widest sense: reciting His name with the tongue, remembrance by the heart, and keeping one's body engaged in complying with the commands of Allah. A narration of ʿĀ'ishah reports that the Prophet ﷺ "used to remember Allah at all times" — and this holds on that wider concept, since he did not make dhikr with his tongue when answering the call of nature, but dhikr by the heart is possible at all times. Shaykh Thānawī distinguishes two types of dhikr by the heart: through "imagined words," and by reflecting and pondering on the divine attributes of perfection.

**Tabattul** is the stronger word. Literally, Maʿārif says, it means "to cut off oneself from the entire creation to focus attention solely on the Creator… and devote oneself exclusively and sincerely to the service of Allah." Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Abū Ṣāliḥ, ʿAṭiyyah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and as-Suddī all glossed it: "This means, make your worship solely for Him alone." Al-Ḥasan: "Strive and devote yourself to Him." Ibn Zayd said *tabattul* signifies "to abandon the world and what is in it and focus attention on what is with Allah." Maʿārif also draws out the practical edge: in all his actions a person should single out Allah for reliance, and should not take any creature as possessing the power of benefit and harm.

Ibn Kathir adds the day-and-night rhythm: make much remembrance of Him and spend your time worshipping Him when you have completed your occupations — as in *"So when you have finished, devote yourself"* (94:7).

**But not monasticism.** Ibn Jarīr notes that a devout worshipper is called *mutabattil*, and that it is reported the Prophet ﷺ forbade *at-tabattul* — which means total devotion to worship while avoiding getting married. Maʿārif sets the same boundary: *rahbāniyyah* (monasticism) is denounced in the Qur'an — *"As for monasticism, it was invented by them"* (57:27) — and Maʿārif cites a hadith denouncing it with the words, "There is no monasticism in Islam." Monasticism means abandoning the world and severing all ties, giving up all lawful and pure things in the belief that doing so *is* worship, and severing human relationships in such a manner that human rights are violated. The *tabattul* of this ayah is something else: **one's relationship with human beings should not overpower his relationship with Allah**, whether in belief or in practice. Such detachment is not contradictory to business relations, or to social contracts and transactions such as marriage and family ties. *Tabattul* in this sense, Maʿārif says, is the characteristic of all the Prophets, and especially of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ; the pious elders alternatively term it *ikhlāṣ*, sincerity.

In the narration quoted above, Saʿīd ibn Hishām had divorced his wife, intending to go out to fight until he died — and he was told that six men of his people had formed that same intention in the Prophet's ﷺ time, upon which he ﷺ said to them: **"Is there not for you all an excellent example in me?"** He forbade them from that, and made them testify that they would take their wives back.

**One point of wording.** The ayah says "remember *the name* of your Lord," not "remember your Lord." Maʿārif, citing Mazharī, takes this as an indication that the repetition of Allah's personal name — *Allah, Allah* — is also a desired and required form of dhikr. It notes that some scholars say such repetition is an innovation (*bidʿah*), and states plainly that **this opinion is not correct** — closing with "And Allah knows best."

## Ayah 9: the Lord of east and west, so lean on Him

*Rabbu'l-mashriqi wa'l-maghribi lā ilāha illā huwa fa'ttakhidhhu wakīlā.* Ibn Kathir explains: He is the Owner and Controller of affairs in the eastern regions and the western regions; He is the One except whom there is no deity worthy of worship. Then he draws the conclusion: **"Just as you single Him out for worship, you should also single Him out for reliance."** Compare *"So worship Him and rely upon Him"* (11:123) and *"You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help"* (1:5).

Maʿārif explains *wakīl* lexically as "a person who has been given a task to do"; to "take Allah as guardian" means that all matters should be entrusted to Allah — technically this is called **tawakkul**, trust. Note the order: preceding this last injunction about trust, Allah's attribute is given — Lord of the East and the West, the only One who can assist in all matters — and *then* the command to rely. *"And whoever places his trust in Allah, He is sufficient for him"* (65:3).

**What tawakkul is not.** Trust in Allah does not imply avoiding the apparent means of acquiring a livelihood, or giving up the normal ways of saving oneself from affliction. On the contrary, to achieve our purpose we must use the powers and causes at our disposal — while not reposing blind faith in material causes and means — and, having taken the actions open to us, leave the result with Allah.

Imam Baghawī, in his *Sharḥ us-Sunnah*, and Bayhaqī, in his *Shuʿab ul-Īmān*, cite the Prophet ﷺ saying: "Jibrā'īl has inspired me with the thought that no person will ever die until he receives, in full, his sustenance that Allah has decreed for him. Therefore, fear Allah and be moderate in your search."

And Tirmidhī transmits a hadith on the authority of Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī that the Prophet ﷺ said: *zuhd* (renunciation of the world) does not mean turning lawful things into unlawful or squandering the wealth Allah has given you; renunciation of the world means **"to have more faith in the things that are in Allah's hands than what are in your hands."**

## Ayah 10: patience, and a parting that stays beautiful

*Waṣbir ʿalā mā yaqūlūna wa'hjurhum hajran jamīlā.* Ibn Kathir states it plainly: Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to be patient with what the foolish among his people who reject him say, and also commands him to keep away from them **"in a nice way… in a way that is not blameworthy."**

*Hajr* literally denotes "to give up something in a state of grief, anger and temper." The rejecters of truth utter words that hurt; he is not to take revenge, but neither is he to maintain relations with them, and at the moment of severing relations it is natural to let slip words of complaint. So the ayah pins the manner down with what Maʿārif calls the grammatically restricted cognate accusative, *hajran jamīlā*: cut the tie, **but maintain your dignity and integrity** — his exalted standard of character requires that he restrain himself from any abusive remark at the deniers of truth.

Following Imam Karkhī, Maʿārif counts this as the sixth injunction given to the Prophet ﷺ, and calls perfect patience the supreme station of *sulūk*: spiritual reformers expend their strength and life on reforming deviant people, and in return hear vile language and are persecuted — and in return they exercise patience in a beautiful manner, not even entertaining the thought of revenge. This supreme station is attained only after *fanā' kāmil*, the complete negation of selfish desires.

**A point on which mufassirūn differ.** Some scholars of tafsir say this verse was repealed by the verses of jihad revealed later. Maʿārif's own conclusion is that it was **not** repealed: patience in the face of what the enemies say, and cutting off from them courteously, are not in conflict with the later verses of reproof, punishment and armed struggle. Jihad is a specific injunction to be applied under specific conditions, and is not a matter of taking revenge or an expression of anger — it is purely acting on the divine command. The injunction of this ayah, Maʿārif holds, "is applicable at all times and under all circumstances."

## Living it

Take some of the night — any voluntary prayer after ʿIshā' fulfils it, the later part after sleep being more virtuous. Keep dhikr running underneath everything, with no laxity — consistency is the point, not intensity. Cut your heart loose from what is not Allah without cutting yourself off from family, trade or obligation. Use every means Allah gave you, and then leave the result with Him. And take both halves of ayah 10 together: patience with what they say, and — if you must step away — a stepping away that stays beautiful.

passages.title: Leave the wealthy deniers to Allah's punishment
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath:** having told His Prophet ﷺ to be patient with what those who reject him among his people say, Allah now turns and says, in effect, *leave them to Me*. Ayat 11–14 are one continuous movement: a warning aimed at a very particular kind of denier (the comfortable, well-provided kind), an account of what is with Allah for them, and the naming of the Day it all falls — the Day the mountains themselves come undone.

The four ayat move as one. Ayah 11 names the people and grants them a short reprieve; ayat 12–13 state what is with Allah for them; ayah 14 names the Day. Ibn Kathir even quotes the end of ayah 13 and the opening of ayah 14 together as a single flow — *"and a painful torment. On the Day when the earth and the mountains will shake"* — because that is how they read.

## The command just before this

Ibn Kathir sets the scene from the previous ayah. In his summary of the passage he renders ayah 10 as **"And be patient with what they say, and keep away from them in a good way,"** and then explains it in his own words: **"Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to be patient with what the foolish who reject him among his people say. Allah also commands him to keep away from them in a nice way. This means in a way that is not blameworthy."**

A withdrawal with no bitterness in it — a keeping-away that carries no blame.

Then, says Ibn Kathir, Allah speaks to him **"as a threat and a warning to his people — and He (Allah) is the Most Great, Whose anger nothing can stand before."** That last phrase is the temperature of the whole passage. Everything that follows is said by the One whose displeasure nothing in creation can absorb or deflect.

## "And leave Me… with the deniers"

Ayah 11 opens with **wa dharnī wa'l-mukadhdhibīn**. Ibn Kathir renders the phrase **"And leave Me alone to deal with the deniers, those who are in possession of good things of life,"** and gives the sense plainly: **"leave Me to deal with the rich rejectors, who own great wealth."**

Feel what this does for the Prophet ﷺ. He is not told to argue harder, to organise a response, or to carry the outcome. The burden is lifted off him and taken up by Allah Himself. His portion is patience and a dignified distance; the reckoning is not his to shoulder. There is real mercy in that division of labour — and real weight in who has taken the other half.

And note who is being handed over: **al-mukadhdhibīn** — rendered in the translation as *the deniers* and by Ibn Kathir as *the rejectors*. They are the same people whose speech the Prophet ﷺ was told to bear patiently: as Ibn Kathir puts it, "the foolish who reject him among his people."

## Why "the people of luxury"?

Ayah 11 does not stop at "the deniers." It adds a description: **ulī an-naʿmah**. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, **"the 'deniers' are referred to as 'the people of luxury.'"**

Maʿārif pauses on the word itself: it is **naʿmah**, the first letter carrying an "a" vowel, and it **"signifies 'ease and plenty; abundance of wealth and children.'"** Not merely money — the whole texture of a cushioned life: means, comfort, family, security, the sense that things are going well.

Maʿārif then draws out why the Qur'an ties this description to denial: *"This indicates that people who live a life of ease, plenty and luxury can only be the ones who deny the Hereafter. These things do often fall to the lot of the believers, but they do not intoxicate them. Therefore, even when they live a life of luxury, their hearts are never, at any time, empty of the thought of the Hereafter. Only the deniers of the Hereafter will live a life of luxury that is neglectful of the Hereafter."*

This is an important and merciful distinction, and it is worth reading twice. **Wealth itself is not the accusation.** Believers receive ease and plenty too. The difference Maʿārif identifies is *intoxication* — whether the comfort empties the heart of the Hereafter or not. The condemned trait is not the bank balance; it is the forgetting that the bank balance made easy. A believer can be rich and still never have a moment when the Hereafter is absent from his heart. That is the line.

Ibn Kathir approaches the same phrase from another side and adds a second reason why the wealthy are singled out: **"For verily, they are more able to obey than others besides them, and they are requested to give the rights (to people) because they have what others do not have."**

So wealth cuts twice. It gives you a greater *capacity* to obey — you can give in ways others simply cannot. And it places *claims* on you: rights owed to people, precisely because you hold what they lack. To be given both the ability and the obligation, and then to deny the One who gave them — that is what makes these particular deniers the ones Allah says "leave to Me."

## "And give them respite for a little"

**wa mahhilhum qalīlā** — Ibn Kathir: *"meaning, for a little while."* He reads it against another ayah:

> *"We let them enjoy for a little, then in the end We shall oblige them to (enter) a great torment."* (31:24)

Notice what this does to the apparent success of the deniers. Their ease is not evidence that Allah has overlooked them; it is a measured, deliberate, and *short* interval — granted, not forgotten. The word **qalīlā** ("a little") is the hinge of the passage: everything they enjoy is on the near side of it, and everything ayat 12–13 describe is on the far side.

## What is "with Us"

Ayah 12 — **inna ladaynā** — is rendered by Ibn Kathir *"Verily, with Us are Ankal, and Jahim,"* and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān *"Surely with Us are fetters and flaming fire, and food that chokes, and a painful punishment."* The two commentaries take the list item by item:

**1. Ankāl.** Ibn Kathir: *"these are fetters"* — and he lists an unusually long chain of authorities who all said so: **Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Tawus, Muhammad bin Kaʿb, ʿAbdullah bin Buraydah, Abu ʿImran al-Jawni, Abu Mijlaz, ad-Dahhak, Hammad bin Abi Sulayman, Qatadah, as-Suddi, Ibn al-Mubarak, ath-Thawri and others.** Maʿārif adds that *ankāl* is the plural of *nakal*, and that it denotes **"fetter, chain, shackle."** When that many of the early authorities converge on a single meaning, the reader can rest on it.

**2. Jahīm.** Ibn Kathir: *"This is a blazing fire."*

**3. Ṭaʿāman dhā ghuṣṣah — food that chokes** (ayah 13). Ibn ʿAbbas explains: *"This means it will get stuck in the throat and it will not enter or come out."* Maʿārif opens the word up: **ghuṣṣah** literally denotes *"a thing by which one is choked"* — *"a morsel may block the throat in such a way as it can neither be swallowed nor can it be brought up."* Anyone who has ever choked on a mouthful knows that particular panic for a few seconds. The ayah holds it there. Maʿārif notes that the inmates of the Fire will be given *"Bariʿ and zaqqum (thorny fruits)"* to eat, and that these fruits fit the description; it records the words of **Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him): "In it will be thorns of fire that will choke."**

**4. ʿAdhāban alīmā — a painful punishment.** Maʿārif reads this closing phrase as deliberately open-ended: *"Having described specific forms of punishment, this description is general — indicating that there will be many more horrible and terrible forms of punishment which man cannot even imagine."* Three named horrors, and then a door left open.

There is a bleak symmetry in the order the passage itself lays down. The people described as *ulī an-naʿmah* — those with freedom of movement, ease, and the best food — are answered with shackles, fire, and a mouthful that will neither go down nor come back up.

## The Day the ground gives way

Ayah 14 names the Day: **yawma tarjufu'l-arḍu wa'l-jibāl** — *"On the Day when the earth and the mountains will shake."* Ibn Kathir glosses **tarjufu** simply: *"meaning, they will quake."* Maʿārif is explicit that this is the timing of everything just described: **"Verse [14] describes that the punishment will take place on the Day when the earth and mountains will shake."**

Then comes the image that lingers: **wa kānat al-jibālu kathīban mahīlā**. Ibn Kathir: *"meaning, they will become like hills of sand after they had been firm rocks. Then they will be utterly destroyed and nothing will remain of them. This will occur until the entire earth becomes a flat land and no curvature will be seen in it. Thus, there will be no valleys and no hills. This means that no part of it will be low or elevated."*

Maʿārif describes the same: the mountains **"will be reduced to a heap of dust or shifting dunes."**

Sit with the sequence Ibn Kathir traces. First the mountains lose their solidity and become poured sand — the substance you cannot stand on, that runs away underfoot. Then even the sand-heaps go, until the earth is a single featureless plain. Ibn Kathir spells out the consequence with unusual precision: *no valleys and no hills, no part of it low or elevated.* Nothing to climb, nothing to shelter behind — the most solid things in a person's world are the first to go.

## How the early Muslims heard these words

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, under the heading *"The Righteous Elders' Fear of the Hereafter,"* reports that **Imam Ahmad, Ibn Abi Dawud, Ibn ʿAdiyy and Baihaqi** record a narration that a person heard this verse and fainted.

It then relates, citing **Ruh ul-Maʿani**, an account of **Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him)**: he was fasting, and when the food was brought to him at the time of iftar, this verse came into his mind and he could not eat, so he sent it away. The following day he was fasting again, and the same thing happened in the evening; again he sent the food away. On the third day, the same. His sons went to **Thabit Bunani, Yazid Dabb, and Yahya al-Bakkaʾ** and recounted the story. All three went to Hasan and insisted on his eating something, and at their insistence he ate a little.

Three things are worth taking from this. First, these ayat were never meant to be read at a comfortable distance — a man of Hasan al-Basri's calibre could not lift a morsel to his mouth while *"food that chokes"* was in his mind. Second, it is a report about the righteous who came after the Prophet ﷺ, not a hadith from him, and Maʿārif presents it as such. Third — and this is the balance — the righteous men around him came and insisted, and he ate. Fear of the Hereafter is meant to reshape a life, not to end it.

## Living it

**If Allah has given you ease, the passage is speaking about you — but not necessarily against you.** Maʿārif's test is not how much you have; it is whether your heart is ever, at any moment, empty of the thought of the Hereafter. Comfort that leaves that thought intact is not what ayah 11 condemns.

**Wealth raises the bar, it does not lower it.** Ibn Kathir's point deserves to be acted on: you are *more able to obey* than others, and there are *rights owed to people* out of what you hold. Ease that produces no giving is exactly the profile ayah 11 draws.

**Their prosperity is not a verdict.** *"Give them respite for a little"* means the interval is granted and counted, not overlooked. Whoever is watching deniers flourish is watching *qalīlā* — a little.

**And when you are the one being rejected, the instruction is not to answer in kind.** Patience with what they say, keeping away in a manner that is not blameworthy, and then — hardest and most freeing — *leave Me with them.* The case belongs to the One whose anger nothing can stand before. That is not your file to carry.

*And Allah knows best.*

passages.title: The Pharaoh precedent and the greying Day
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is doing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sums these ayat up in a line: they "describe the horrors and terrors of the Day of Resurrection." Ayat 15–18 make a single argument in four moves: a messenger has been sent to you exactly as a messenger was sent to Pharaoh; you know how Pharaoh's story ended; so if you deny, what shelter do you imagine you have — either from a seizure like his, or from a Day that turns children grey and splits the sky open? Then ayah 19 releases the pressure and turns the whole warning into an open door: *this is a reminder — so whoever wills, let him take a path to his Lord.*

## "A witness over you" (ayah 15)

Ibn Kathir gives this stretch of the surah its own heading, and the heading is itself the argument: your Messenger ﷺ is like the messenger who was sent to Pharaoh — and you know what happened to Pharaoh.

He notes that at this point Allah "addresses the disbelievers of the Quraysh, and along with them the rest of mankind." That last phrase matters for how you read the passage today: the Quraysh are the first audience, but not the only one.

The messenger is described as *shāhidan ʿalaykum* — **a witness over you**. Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and heavy: "witnessing your deeds." What he is a witness to is not an idea or an era. It is what you did.

Notice how the ayah is built. The two sendings are set inside a single sentence, the second phrased as a mirror of the first: *Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh.* Maʿārif ul Qurʾān states the parallel plainly: Allah sent a Messenger, Muḥammad ﷺ, to bear witness against the pagans of Makkah just as He sent a Messenger, Mūsā (peace be upon him), to Pharaoh. The comparison is not decoration. It is the whole point, and the next ayah collects on it.

## The Pharaoh precedent (ayat 15–16)

*fa-ʿaṣā firʿawnu-r-rasūla fa-akhadhnāhu akhdhan wabīlā* — "But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger, so We seized him with a severe seizure," in Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's rendering. On the word *wabīl*, Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, as-Suddī and ath-Thawrī all explained it as **severe**.

Ibn Kathir's own paraphrase catches the tone of it: "Allah seized him with the seizing of One Mighty and Powerful." And he connects the moment to Allah's words elsewhere about Pharaoh, *So Allah seized him with punishment for his last and first transgression* (79:25).

**The argument the ayah is making.** Ibn Kathir spells out the reasoning the listener is meant to complete himself: "you should beware of denying this Messenger, lest you be afflicted by that which befell Fir'awn." And then he reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid a sharper form of the same point — since your Messenger ﷺ is more noble and greater than Prophet Mūsā the son of ʿImrān, you would be *even more* deserving of destruction and ruin if you deny him.

The logic runs from the lesser to the greater. If refusing Mūsā (peace be upon him) brought down what it brought down on Pharaoh, what does refusing a greater messenger deserve? The ayah does not finish the sentence. It leaves the listener to finish it, which is far more uncomfortable than being told.

## Two levels of warning (ayat 16–17)

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws out the structure very clearly, and it is worth following slowly. Pharaoh, it notes, was seized with terrible severity "right in this world."

So the first warning is worldly: likewise, if the pagans of Makkah persist stubbornly in their conduct, they too can be seized with terrible severity in this very world.

And then the second warning closes the last exit: even if no torment is inflicted in this world, no one can escape the horrors, the terrors, and the sheer length of the Day of Resurrection — the Day that turns the children grey.

That is the hinge into ayah 17. The first door is bolted; the second is shown to have no handle on our side at all.

## The greying Day (ayah 17)

*fa-kayfa tattaqūna in kafartum yawman yajʿalu-l-wildāna shībā* — "Then how can you protect yourselves from the punishment, if you disbelieve, on a Day that will make the children grey-headed?"

**How to read the question.** Ibn Kathir records that Ibn Jarīr cited the recitation of Ibn Masʿūd, which renders the sense: "How can you, O people, fear a Day that makes the children grey-headed, if you disbelieve in Allah and do not testify to Him?" Ibn Kathir then lays out two readings:

1. *How can you attain safety for yourselves from the Day of this great horror, if you disbelieve?*
2. *How can you attain piety at all, if you disbelieve in the Day of Judgement and reject it?* — that is, what reverence for Allah can there be in someone who denies the reckoning?

Ibn Kathir's verdict: "Both of these meanings are good. However, the first interpretation is closer to the truth. And Allah knows best." That closing formula is worth noticing — a scholar of his standing weighing two valid readings, preferring one, and still leaving the final word to Allah.

Either way, the question is rhetorical in the strongest sense. It does not ask *whether* you have protection; it asks you to name it, knowing you cannot.

**Why children go grey.** Ibn Kathir explains the image as caused by "the severity of its horrors, its earthquakes and its disturbing confusion." Grey hair is what long years produce — Maʿārif ul Qurʾān renders the phrase as a day that turns "the small boys into grey-headed old men." Here it arrives on the young, in a day.

At this point Ibn Kathir attaches a report about the enormity of that Day: Allah will say to Ādam, "Send a group to the Fire." Ādam will say, "How many?" And Allah will reply, "From every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire, and one to Paradise." Ibn Kathir cites this here without naming a collection, so it is passed on exactly as he passes it on — as an indication of the sheer weight of that Day, not as a licence to despair. The passage itself ends by pointing the reader toward a path, not away from one.

**Metaphor or literal?** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records that scholars differed here. The greying of children, it says, "could be a metaphor for the most calamitous happenings which bring about disastrous changes" — the way any language speaks of an event that ages a person. "But some scholars say that this is a description of reality, in that the Day of Resurrection will be so long that a little child will grow old," and it points to Qurṭubī and Rūḥ for the discussion. Both positions are held by respected scholars; the warning of the ayah stands on either reading, and there is no need to force a choice between them.

## The sky comes apart (ayah 18)

*as-samāʾu munfaṭirun bihi* — "whereon the heaven will be cleft asunder." Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah both explained the little word *bihi*: it means "because of it (the Day of Judgement), due to its severity and its horror." So the splitting of the sky is not merely something that happens *on* that Day; it is caused by it. The Day is heavy enough that the heavens themselves give way under it.

Then the passage seals it: *kāna waʿduhu mafʿūlā* — "His promise is certainly to be accomplished." Ibn Kathir: the promise of this Day will be fulfilled — "it will occur and there is no way around it, and it will come to pass and there is no avoiding it." After an ayah that asks *how will you protect yourselves*, this removes the last comfort a listener might reach for: the hope that the Day is talk rather than appointment.

## The door left open (ayah 19)

*inna hādhihi tadhkirah* — "Verily, this is an admonition." Ibn Kathir says "this" refers to **this Surah**, and that it is an admonition in the sense that men of understanding receive admonition from it. So the whole of Sūrah al-Muzzammil is gathered up and handed to the listener as one reminder.

*fa-man shāʾa-ttakhadha ilā rabbihi sabīlā* — "therefore whosoever wills, let him take a path to his Lord." The wording is striking after four ayat of warning. No compulsion is applied; a road is simply pointed out and left open. And notice the destination: not a path to safety, but *a path to his Lord* — **rabbihi**, his own Lord. The Fire has been described; what is offered is not merely escape from it but a road that leads to Him.

**Human will and Allah's will.** Ibn Kathir immediately balances the ayah so that no one misreads it as human choice operating on its own. "Whoever wills," he says, means "from those whom Allah wills that they be guided," and he calls this a stipulation Allah mentions elsewhere, bringing the ayah that makes it explicit: *But you cannot will, unless Allah wills. Verily Allah is Ever All-Knowing, All-Wise* (76:30).

Both halves are to be held together, exactly as Ibn Kathir holds them: the invitation is real and it is addressed to you — *whoever wills* — and at the same time no one wills anything outside the will of Allah, who is All-Knowing and All-Wise. The believer's response to this is not speculation but supplication: to ask Allah for the willing, and then to walk.

## Living it

**Take the address personally.** Ibn Kathir explicitly widened the audience of ayah 15 beyond the Quraysh to "the rest of mankind," and the messenger's role is described as "witnessing your deeds." That is a sobering thought, and also a dignifying one: your life is not unobserved and unweighed.

**Read the precedent as it was meant.** Ibn Kathir states the takeaway in one line: beware of denying this Messenger ﷺ, lest you be afflicted by what befell Pharaoh. The story is not told as ancient history; it is told as a pattern, and the ayah expects you to see yourself somewhere inside it.

**Do not treat the Day as a distant rumour.** *His promise is certainly to be accomplished* is the passage's flat answer to the part of us that files the Ākhirah under "later." Ibn Kathir's phrasing is worth memorising: there is no way around it, and no avoiding it.

**Then walk the road.** The passage does not end in terror; it ends in ayah 19 with a path and an open invitation. Whatever that Day brings, the response asked of us today is small and immediate: take one step toward your Lord, and ask Him for the will to take the next.

passages.title: The night vigil eased, prayer and charity confirmed
passages.tafsir:
This single long ayah closes Sūrah al-Muzzammil by lifting the burden its opening had placed. The night vigil that had been prescribed as an obligation is relaxed into what is easy, and in its place three duties are named and confirmed: the prescribed prayer, zakāh, and a goodly loan advanced to Allah. What holds ayah 20 together is a single movement — from *your Lord knows*, to *so He turned to you in mercy*, to *now do this instead*.

## The year of standing that came before

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the opening command of the sūrah — "stand at night (for prayer)" — prescribed the night prayer for Allah's Messenger ﷺ as well as for the general body of Muslims. It was also obligatory for the prayer to be long, though they had a choice in its length: half the night, or a third of it, or two-thirds.

A group of the noble Companions mostly followed the *ʿazīmah* — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses as "the preferred original rule of law." As a result they spent almost two-thirds of the night in prayer, every night. During the day they would invite people to Islam, preach, and attend to their personal needs; most of the Companions were either labourers or businessmen. The Messenger's ﷺ feet, as well as the Companions' feet, would swell on account of the long prayers.

Allah was fully aware of the entire set-up, and it was pre-decreed in His knowledge that the difficulty was temporary. The purpose of the exercise, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, was *riyāḍah* — "ascetic discipline." In the initial stages they were in a condition of disequilibrium; therefore they were required to exert themselves in spiritual struggle and ascetic discipline, as the sūrah itself had said: "**We are going to send down to you a weighty discourse**" (73:5). The Prophet ﷺ was going to be handed the service of the Qurʼān, which is much more difficult than this ascetic discipline. And when the ascetic discipline was completed and by His grace perfect balance was attained, asceticism was replaced by moderation — and the obligatory nature of the night prayer was repealed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the timing. The abrogating passage was revealed one year or eight months after the initial verses of this sūrah. It reports that the Musnad of Aḥmad, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah and Nasāʼī record a narration of Sayyidah ʿĀʼishah, who stated that at the commencement of this sūrah Allah had prescribed the night prayer; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the blessed Companions constantly carried out the obligation for a year; Allah held back the last part of the sūrah in the sky for twelve months; and it was revealed after a year, abrogating the obligatory status of the night prayer and reducing its status to supererogation. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tags this report *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*.)

So ayah 20 is no abstract legal clause. It is the answer, delivered after about a year, to a strain of which Allah was fully aware the whole time.

## "Surely your Lord knows" — relief framed as knowledge

The ayah opens not with a command, not with a rebuke, but with knowledge: *your Lord knows that you do stand a little less than two-thirds of the night, or half the night, or a third of the night, and also a party of those with you.*

Ibn Kathīr reads this as a description of what was actually happening: "sometimes like this and sometimes like that, and all of these are done unintentionally. However, you all are not able to be consistent with the night prayer Allah has commanded you, because it is difficult for you."

And then: "**And Allah measures the night and the day**" — meaning, says Ibn Kathīr, that sometimes the night and day are equal, and sometimes one of them is longer or shorter than the other. The very thing they were trying to divide into thirds was itself being lengthened and shortened by Allah.

## عَلِمَ أَن لَّن تُحۡصُوهُ — "He knows that you cannot do it regularly"

Ibn Kathīr's gloss here is brief and pointed: He knows that you are unable to pray the whole night — "meaning, the obligation which He prescribed for you."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works on the word itself. *Iḥṣāʼ* literally denotes **"to count."** It records two ways commentators have taken the phrase.

**First:** Allah had not fixed the exact time for the night prayer. The Companions were given the option of choosing a time between one-third of the night and two-thirds of it. But when they were preoccupied with the prayer, it was difficult for them to calculate whether they had stayed up half the night, or a third, or two-thirds, because in those days there were no watches or clocks to measure the time. Even if there had been, it was not in keeping with their condition to look at the time repeatedly; they would be absorbed in their prayers, oblivious to their environment.

**Second:** other scholars say *iḥṣāʼ* connotes the act of counting in the sense that Allah knows you will not be able to keep count of the constant prayers through those lengthy hours. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word carries this fuller sense in a hadith it cites in connection with the beautiful names of Allah — "He who keeps count of them will enter Paradise" — where keeping count means acting fully in accordance with the attributes and qualities of Allah as indicated in His beautiful names. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does not name a collection for this report.) The same word appears in "**And if you count the bounties of Allah, you cannot count them all**" (14:34).

## فَتَابَ عَلَيۡكُمۡ — "therefore He turned to you in mercy"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a lovely detail of language. The word *tawbah* originally means **"to turn."** Repentance for sins is also called *tawbah* in Arabic, because the sinner turns away from his past sins and crimes — but in this context the word simply means "to turn": that is, Allah took back the obligatory nature of the injunction of the night prayer.

## "So, recite you of the Qurʼān as much as may be easy"

Ibn Kathīr explains that the instruction is deliberately unfixed: "without specification of any set time." This means, he says, stand and pray during the night as much as is easy for you.

He also notes a point of Qurʼānic usage worth learning: **Allah uses the term recitation (*qirāʼah*) to mean prayer (*ṣalāh*).** His evidence is Sūrah al-Isrāʼ — "And offer your Salah neither aloud" (17:110), where Ibn Kathīr comments, "meaning, your recitation," and "Nor in low voice" (17:110). So "recite what is easy" is an instruction to *pray* at night to whatever extent you can.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the practical consequence. What is recited here is the tahajjud prayer, which is no longer obligatory; it is supererogatory, enjoying the status of *sunnah* or *mustaḥabb* (recommended). No particular number of verses has been fixed for recitation of the Qurʼān in tahajjud: every person may perform the prayer according to his own ability in the time available to him. The sūrah that began by asking for two-thirds of the night ends by asking for whatever you have.

## The excuses Allah names for you

Then comes something remarkable — Allah Himself names the situations in which a believer may not manage the night prayer. Ibn Kathīr comments that He knows there will be people of this nation who will have excuses for not praying the voluntary night prayer: those who are ill and therefore not able to perform it; those travelling in the land seeking the bounty of Allah in business and trade; and others who will be busy with that which is more important to them, an example being going on expeditions to fight in the way of Allah.

Two things are worth pausing on. First, honest trade is here described as "seeking of Allah's bounty" — the merchant's journey stands among the recognised excuses. Second, Ibn Kathīr's own observation: this entire sūrah was revealed in Makkah **even though fighting was not legislated until after it was revealed**. Thus, he says, it is among the greatest of the signs of prophethood, because it informs about unseen matters of the future.

## What "abrogation" actually means here

Because this passage is the classic case of *naskh* (abrogation), Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses to clear up a misunderstanding. Human legislatures repeal laws for two kinds of reason: either the legislators did not fully comprehend the situation when they framed the law and must amend it when they realise circumstances have changed, or they simply did not foresee that circumstances might change at all, so the old law must be repealed and a new one promulgated. **It is inconceivable that these two forms of repeal will ever apply to divine injunctions.**

There is a third case, and it is the only one that has taken place in divine injunctions: the legislator foresees from the outset that in time conditions will change so that the law will no longer apply in full, and when the conditions alter he legislates and makes public the new law, as he had forethought. It has always been the case, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, that a certain piece of divine law was intended from the very beginning to remain in force for a limited time, but divine wisdom chose not to disclose that time limit to people. Because of the general wording of the legislation, the community took it for an immutable law, whereas Allah had pre-decreed it as temporary. When its period was over the law was withdrawn. People took this as the abrogation of a law, whereas in reality it merely made publicly known that the law had been promulgated for a limited term, and that the term was now over.

Ibn Kathīr reports that **Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and others from the Salaf** said: "Verily, this Ayah abrogated the standing for prayer at night that Allah previously made obligatory for the Muslims."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a further view according to Ibn ʿAbbās, in which the relief came in two stages: these verses merely cancelled the obligatory nature of the night prayer, while the basic tahajjud prayer remained intact as obligatory; and when the five daily prayers were prescribed on the night of the Ascent (*miʿrāj*), the obligatory nature of tahajjud too was cancelled — "and Allah knows best."

A question is also raised about the Prophet ﷺ in particular, because of the phrase *nāfilatan lak*, "an additional prayer for you." The word *nāfilah* literally denotes "additional," and is used here in its technical sense of *nafl*, "supererogatory." If tahajjud is a *nafl* prayer for all, it is not clear why the wording adds *lak*, "for you." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that **according to the overwhelming majority, the correct view is that the obligatory nature of the tahajjud prayer has been abrogated for Allah's Messenger ﷺ as well as for the general body of Muslims, while it still remains an act of supererogation for all** — and refers the reader to its own fuller treatment of whether tahajjud is a mere *nafl* or a *sunnah muʼakkadah*.

## What is confirmed in its place: prayer, zakāh, and a loan to Allah

The ayah does not merely lighten; it fixes what remains binding. "**And perform Salah and give Zakah**" — Ibn Kathīr: establish your obligatory prayers and pay your obligatory zakāh.

On the prayer, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that according to the majority of the commentators, *ṣalāh* in this context refers to the five prescribed prayers that were made obligatory on the Night of Ascent — citing **Ibn Kathīr, Qurṭubī and al-Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ**. This indicates the sequence: the night prayer was obligatory for a year; in the meantime the nocturnal journey took place and the five daily prayers were prescribed; after that these verses were revealed and the obligatory nature of tahajjud was abrogated. Ibn Kathīr cites here what **has been confirmed in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs**, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to a man, "Five obligatory prayers during a day and a night (are obligatory)." The man said, "Is there anything other than this (of prayer) that is obligatory upon me?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ replied, "No, except what you may do voluntarily."

On zakāh there is a well-known difficulty, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states plainly: zakāh here refers to the prescribed zakāh, yet it is popularly understood that zakāh was prescribed two years after the migration to Madīnah, whereas this verse is Makkan — and a consensus of scholarly opinion assigns the revelation of this sūrah to the earliest period of the call. In response, some commentators express the view that this particular verse was revealed in Madīnah. **Ibn Kathīr, however, says** that zakāh was prescribed in the earliest days of Islam, although its details — like the exemption limit (*niṣāb*, the threshold at which wealth becomes zakātable) and the rate — were fixed in the second year of migration at Madīnah — "and Allah knows best." So the word may be taken in its technical sense of prescribed zakāh even in a Makkan verse.

## وَأَقۡرِضُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ قَرۡضًا حَسَنًا — "and advance to Allah a goodly loan"

Ibn Kathīr glosses "lend to Allah a handsome loan" as meaning **from charitable donations** — "for verily, Allah will reward for this the best and most abundant of rewards" — and cites the parallel: "**Who is he that will lend to Allah a goodly loan so that He may multiply it to him many times?**" (2:245).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on the courtesy of the image. To spend in the way of Allah as charitable donations is spoken of as though one were advancing a loan to Allah. This indicates divine favour and grace toward the giver, and it also describes that **Allah is the richest of all**: the loan will not be lost, but will be richly returned.

Since the command for zakāh has already been mentioned previously, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out that advancing a loan to Allah refers — **according to most scholars** — to other voluntary charitable donations in the cause of Allah, as for instance spending on friends and relatives, or using one's wealth for the entertainment of guests, or investing it in the service of scholars and righteous people. Some scholars point out that besides the prescribed zakāh there are other financial obligations imposed on a man, such as the maintenance of parents, wife and children; on that view, "give the zakāh" covers the prescribed due, while "advance to Allah a goodly loan" covers these other financial obligations.

## "Whatever good you send before you for yourselves"

Ibn Kathīr's gloss is simple and piercing: for all that you send before yourselves, you will get it back, and it will be better than what you kept for yourselves in the worldly life.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes it concrete. If a man does good in his lifetime, it is better for him than advising someone else to do the good deed at the time of his death. That applies to financial worship and voluntary charitable donations, and it applies also to prescribed prayers, fasts and other prescribed worship or duties that were missed out or neglected: it is better to pay out the *fidyah* and/or *kaffārah* with one's own hands while one is living, rather than expecting the heirs to discharge it. They may do it, or they may neglect to do it.

Ibn Kathīr reports a hadith that al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Yaʿlā al-Mawṣilī reported from al-Ḥārith bin Suwayd, from ʿAbdullāh, and notes that **al-Bukhārī also recorded this hadith**. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Which of you hold his wealth to be more beloved to him than the wealth of his heir?" They said, "O Messenger of Allah! There is not a single one of us who does not hold his wealth to be more beloved to him than the wealth of his heir." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then said: "Know what you are saying!" They replied, "What do we know other than this, O Messenger of Allah?" He then said: "**The wealth of one of you is only that which he sends forth, and the wealth of his heir is that which he leaves behind.**"

## And the last word: seek forgiveness

The ayah — and the sūrah — closes with "**And seek forgiveness of Allah. Verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most-Merciful.**" Ibn Kathīr explains: remember Him and seek forgiveness from Him often for all of your matters, for verily He is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful to whoever seeks His forgiveness.

A community had spent a year standing in the night until their feet swelled — and still the passage closes by telling them to remember Allah and seek His forgiveness often, in all their affairs, and seals the sūrah with two names: *al-Ghafūr* and *ar-Raḥīm*.

## Living it

- **Take the easy portion, and take it.** The ayah's own standard is *mā tayassara* — what is easy. Pray according to your ability, in the time available to you.
- **Guard the five, and guard the zakāh.** These are what the ayah establishes as binding after the relief.
- **Give beyond the zakāh** — to relatives and friends, to guests, to those who serve knowledge and religion — knowing that most scholars read the "goodly loan" as exactly this, and that a loan advanced to Allah is not lost but richly returned.
- **Settle your accounts yourself.** Missed or neglected obligations, the *fidyah* or *kaffārah* owed, charity you meant to give: better to discharge it with your own hands while you live than to leave it to heirs who may do it or may neglect it.
- **Seek Allah's forgiveness often, for all your matters** — the last instruction of the sūrah.
